precepts.text: In his own synagogue they said, is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James and Joses and Juda and Simon, and are not his sisters here with us? They knew his family and were offended at him.
precepts.point: Israel named sons the same name: Mattathias had Joannan and Jonathan, there were three Marys at the cross and Simons everywhere, so two Zerubbabels is no puzzle.

note.label: The Nativity: the Bloodline, Birthright, & the Messiah

precepts.why:
Mark gives the same account as Matthew 13. On the sabbath Christ “began to teach in the synagogue: and many hearing him were astonished, saying, From whence hath this man these things?” Then: “Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James, and Joses, and of Juda, and Simon? and are not his sisters here with us? And they were offended at him.”

They knew his family. They knew his background, his mother, his brothers by name, and his sisters. Who do he think he is? We grew up with this guy. He ain't nobody special. You're from the hood like us, from Nazareth; what you talking about, Savior? In his own home, where he was from, he got disrespected by his own neighbors and family members.

So the scripture itself shows Christ was born into a real family, the son of Mary with brothers and sisters, and that the people offended at him were the ones who knew exactly where he came from.

precepts.text: Paul says to Agrippa, I know thee to be expert in all customs and questions which are among the Jews.
precepts.point: John had told Herod plainly, It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother's wife. Herod knew the law well enough to be accused by it, because those rulers were schooled in the customs of Israel.

note.label: Mark 6: A Prophet Without Honour, the Death of John, and the Five Thousand

precepts.why:
Herod hears of Christ and says, “It is John, whom I beheaded: he is risen from the dead.” He had bound John in prison for Herodias' sake, his brother Philip's wife, “For John had said unto Herod, It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother’s wife.”

John told him plainly it was not lawful, and Herod knew the law well enough to be accused by it. Those rulers were schooled in the customs of Israel. Paul says as much to Agrippa: “Especially because I know thee to be expert in all customs and questions which are among the Jews: wherefore I beseech thee to hear me patiently.” Agrippa was expert in all the customs and questions among the Jews, and Herod was no different. He was not ignorant of the law he broke; he knew it, took his brother's wife anyway, and then took John's head.

points: In his own country they are astonished at his wisdom and his mighty works, and then are offended at him because they know his family.

note.label: Mark 6: A Prophet Without Honour, the Death of John, and the Five Thousand

points: A prophet is not without honour, but in his own country, and among his own kin, and in his own house. What was done to him is done to those teaching today: men who knew you before you repented ask who you think you are.

note.label: Mark 6: A Prophet Without Honour, the Death of John, and the Five Thousand

points: He could there do no mighty work, save that he laid his hands upon a few sick folk and healed them, and he marvelled because of their unbelief.

note.label: Mark 6: A Prophet Without Honour, the Death of John, and the Five Thousand

points: He sends them forth by two and two with power over unclean spirits, taking nothing for the journey but a staff.

note.label: Mark 6: A Prophet Without Honour, the Death of John, and the Five Thousand

points: Whosoever will not receive you nor hear you, shake off the dust under your feet for a testimony against them. The word goes out whether they hear or whether they forbear, and that shaking of the dust seals the judgment.

note.label: Mark 6: A Prophet Without Honour, the Death of John, and the Five Thousand

points: Herod hears of him and says it is John, whom he beheaded, risen from the dead.

note.label: Mark 6: A Prophet Without Honour, the Death of John, and the Five Thousand

points: John had told Herod plainly, It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother's wife. Herod knew the law well enough to be accused by it, because those rulers were schooled in the customs of Israel.

note.label: Mark 6: A Prophet Without Honour, the Death of John, and the Five Thousand

points: Herodias had a quarrel against John and would have killed him, but could not, for Herod feared him, knowing that he was a just man and an holy.

note.label: Mark 6: A Prophet Without Honour, the Death of John, and the Five Thousand

points: When the oath is made, the daughter asks her mother what to ask, and is told, The head of John the Baptist. The king was exceeding sorry, but for his oath's sake he sent the executioner.

note.label: Mark 6: A Prophet Without Honour, the Death of John, and the Five Thousand

points: He was moved with compassion toward them, because they were as sheep not having a shepherd, and he began to teach them many things.

note.label: Mark 6: A Prophet Without Honour, the Death of John, and the Five Thousand

points: He made them sit down by companies, in ranks by hundreds and by fifties. No man argued about where he was placed. The Most High is a God of order, and the eating came after the order.

note.label: Mark 6: A Prophet Without Honour, the Death of John, and the Five Thousand

points: Five loaves and two fishes feed five thousand men, and twelve baskets of fragments are taken up.

note.label: Mark 6: A Prophet Without Honour, the Death of John, and the Five Thousand

points: He comes to them walking upon the sea, and they suppose it had been a spirit and cry out. These were fishermen; they knew what water does.

note.label: Mark 6: A Prophet Without Honour, the Death of John, and the Five Thousand

points: They were sore amazed, for they considered not the miracle of the loaves, for their heart was hardened. Men can watch a thing done in front of them and still not take it to heart.

note.label: Mark 6: A Prophet Without Honour, the Death of John, and the Five Thousand

points: Wherever he entered, they laid the sick in the streets and besought him that they might touch if it were but the border of his garment, and as many as touched him were made whole.
